results.caption: Back in 2024, Chinese marathon runner Li Meizhen got her period in the middle of a marathon—but it didn’t stop her from finishing.  The incident happened during the Hengshui Lake Marathon, where Li unexpectedly got her period around the 34-kilometre mark. Despite blood running down her legs, she continued and crossed the finish line in 2 hours and 35 minutes. After the race, Li explained she was already so close to the finish line that she didn’t want to withdraw. She also needed to complete two championship marathons that season to earn points for her team, meaning dropping out would have meant running another full marathon later. The footage quickly went viral across China, with many calling Li’s determination deeply inspiring. It also sparked wider conversations about breaking the stigma around menstruation in sport. 💭 What do you think?👇🏼 #womenempowerment #womensports #period #marathon #storytime

results.caption: For more than a decade, auxiliary police officer Shi Dongliang has been a familiar face outside a primary school in Guanyun County, Jiangsu Province, helping generations of children cross the road safely. Shi joined the police auxiliary force in 1999 and has been assigned to the school crossing since 2013. Every day, he arrives before students, walking around 20,000 steps as he runs back and forth directing traffic—covering roughly 1,500 kilometres each year. His dedication has earned him the nickname "Running Brother" (奔跑哥). In 2019, videos of him tirelessly running across the crossing went viral on Douyin, introducing his story to millions across China. Over the years, parents have thanked him with letters, children have slipped snacks into his pockets, and graduating classes have insisted he stand at the centre of their class photos. "The children's safety is what matters most," Shi says. "Running back and forth is tiring, but as long as I can keep an eye on every vehicle and every child, I feel at ease. I hope they all grow up safe, learn to protect themselves, and learn to help others." ❤️ #police #policeofficer #school #storytime #hearttouching

results.transcript: I've had bowed legs my whole life. Ever since I can remember, my mother would lament, why couldn't you get my skinny thighs or my narrow feet? Why did you have to inherit my crooked legs? I'd stand in front of the mirror and try my best to bring my knees together without bending them to my brother good, but no matter how hard I tried, they never touched. My mother was bullied for her bowed legs. The kids would laugh and point and say she couldn't walk in a straight line. And so starting from when I could speak, Amma always told me to walk in a straight line. I got made fun of too. In junior high, the kids would call me born on a horse. And once I even overheard my friend tell someone, Joanne's pretty, but her legs are really messed up. In high school, my mom dropped thousands of dollars on these custom braces from Korea that were supposedly designed to straighten my legs. Think Forrest Gump. I had to wear them every night while I slept and they were hot and sticky and they hurt. For an entire summer, I stayed up all night, hating my mom, hating the braces, hating my legs, until she finally relented and we gave up on the braces. Nowadays, every time someone tries to make me feel self-conscious about my legs, I ask them one simple question. I've run five marathons. How many have you? I've run five marathons.
